'''Harry Pollard''' (28 February 1919 – November 20, 1985)<ref name="cm">{{citation|title=In Memorian. Professor Harry Pollard. 1919-1985|last=Saari|first=D. G.|authorlink = Donald G. Saari|journal=Celestial Mechanics|year=1985 |volume=37|page=349|bibcode=1985CeMec..37..349S|issue=4|mr=0846726|doi=10.1007/bf01261623|s2cid=189832088 }}.</ref> was an American mathematician.  He received his PhD from [[Harvard University]] in 1942 under the supervision of [[David Widder]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=17808|title=Harry Pollard}}</ref> He then taught at [[Cornell University]], and was professor of mathematics at [[Purdue University]] from 1961 until his death in 1985. He is known for his work on [[celestial mechanics]], [[orthogonal polynomials]] and the [[n-body problem]]<ref name="cm"/> as well as for the several textbooks he authored or co-authored.<ref name="w51"/><ref name="k73"/> In the theory of Orthogonal polynomials, Pollard solved a conjecture of [[Antoni Zygmund]], establishing mean convergence of the partial sums in <math>L^p</math> norms for the [[Legendre polynomials]] and [[Jacobi polynomials]] in a series of three papers in the Transactions of the American Mathematical Society. The first of these papers deals with the fundamental case of [[Legendre polynomials]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Pollard, Harry.|title=The Mean Convergence of Orthogonal Series I|journal= Transactions of the American Mathematical Society| volume=62|issue=3|year=1947|pages=387–403|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1947-0022932-1 |doi-access=free}}</ref> The end point case in Pollard's theorem was established by [[Sagun Chanillo]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Chanillo, Sagun| title=On the Weak Behaviour of Partial Sums of Legendre Series|journal= Transactions of the American Mathematical Society|volume=268|issue=2|year=1981|pages=367–376|doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1981-0632534-1|doi-access=free}}</ref>
